title: No more heated seat subscriptions for cars in New York from 2027
gist: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed S.9348A/A.10411A, banning automakers, dealers and third parties from charging subscriptions or post-purchase fees for features using pre-installed hardware with no ongoing cost, effective February 27, 2027. Gitlin argues the 'ongoing cost' wording leaves a large loophole for map-, data- and software-dependent features like navigation, hands-free driving, OnStar or Mercedes' Drive Assist Pro.

insights.claim: New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law banning car companies and dealerships from locking vehicle features behind subscriptions, effective February 27, 2027.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: State-level regulation is starting to cap automaker recurring-revenue strategies; watch for copycat states.

insights.claim: Bill S.9348A/A.10411A prohibits manufacturers, dealers and third-party providers from charging subscription or post-purchase fees for any vehicle feature that uses pre-installed hardware without an ongoing cost.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: The 'no ongoing cost' test is the crux that determines which revenue streams survive.

insights.claim: Automakers pursue connected-car subscriptions largely because capital markets reward recurring revenue, with monthly payments and sellable driver data being the real goal behind features like remote start.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Explains why software/subscription revenue is central to OEM valuation narratives and why regulation threatens it.

insights.claim: BMW's heated-seat subscription was only offered in markets like South Korea and the UK, never in North America, and in 2023 BMW's board said subscriptions would be limited to software-related features.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Hardware-feature subscriptions already face consumer backlash; software features are where OEMs are retreating to.

insights.claim: The New York law's 'ongoing cost' exemption likely leaves room for fees on enhanced navigation and hands-free driving, because maps and databases require constant updates that create ongoing costs for automakers.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Software- and data-backed ADAS/navigation subscriptions likely remain monetizable despite the ban.

insights.claim: Although BMW-style seat-heater subscriptions will be barred in New York, services such as GM's OnStar or Mercedes' Drive Assist Pro may still carry ongoing fees under the new law.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Limited near-term revenue impact on OEM connected-service businesses.
